newsitem.title: UK: What world backing for Zaire relief force?.
newsitem.headline: What world backing for Zaire relief force?.

text.p: France and Spain have proposed sending a multi-national force to ensure aid gets through to the thousands of refugees fleeing ethnic conflict in eastern Zaire.
At a meeting in Madrid on Wednesday they suggested sending 5,000 troops to open humanitarian routes to help the refugees, some of whom are already dying of thirst and starvation.

But what countries will overcome their reluctance to provide troops and get involved in what is seen as an intractable African conflict? FRANCE - First reports said Paris will provide 1,000 troops as the core of the mission to the region where France has long held influence and has sent forces in the recent past. But French military officials say that number could change.

They add that France will take care the force be seen as neutral to save Paris from the scandal which followed its unilateral mission to Rwanda in 1994 which Tutsis said served to protect Hutus guilty of the genocide of their kinsfolk. SPAIN - Madrid joined France in making the original proposal and says it will despatch a number of soldiers less than 1,000 UNITED STATES - Both France and Spain called on Washington to help by sending troops to the area. But, distracted by the presidential election, mindful of the Somalia debacle and suspicious of French motives, the U.S. has declined to send soldiers, though it says it may back the force diplomatically. ETHIOPIA - The third country to actually commit troops, it could become part of the African force that France and Spain wants to gradually move in and take over from Western soldiers. BRITAIN - Britain has discussed the idea with Paris and there will be further talks at a summit between Prime minister John Major and President Jacques Chirac in Bordeaux on Thursday. But officials say they are not gearing up to send troops.
"We have no immediate plans for military deployment," a spokesman for the Foreign Office said.

Britain is thought to want more detail on the force's mandate and organisation before thinking of sending soldier. ITALY - Italy says it will wait for a request from the U.N. Security Council before making a decision. "We want to react in a...coordinated fashion with other countries," said Italian Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini. GERMANY - Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel is due to tell the German parliament on Thursday afternoon whether Bonn will send troops or offer logistical support for the force. BELGIUM - Brussels says it will not send soldiers. It says its former colonial rule of the area and the deaths of its soldiers on U.N. duty in Rwanda in 1994 rule out participation. FINLAND, GREECE and other smaller European countries say their position depends on the outcome of Thursday's meeting of EU aid ministers in Brussels IRELAND - Dublin says it supports the Franco-Spanish initiative in principle, provided the force is impartial, but has not decided how it would contribute OTHERS - If the multi-national force proposal was adopted by the United Nations or the Organisation of African Unity other countries might come forward.
